newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: RTRS-Australia dlr deadlocked by US$, up on crosses.
newsitem.headline: RTRS-Australia dlr deadlocked by US$, up on crosses.

text.p: The Australian dollar put in a steady performance against its U.S. counterpart Thursday while offshore developments left it firmer on most crosses.

The day was dominated by fallout from Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan's reminder that U.S. rates may have to rise some time, which pushed yields up sharply here so indirectly supporting the A$. Japanese repatriation also caused ripples as the mark was dumped and yen carried home.
Data on business investment were softer than expected for Q4 but still positive on the outlook for 96/97 and 97/98, while a moderation in private sector wages boded well for low inflation.
By 5.00 pm (0600 GMT) the local dollar was settling in at US$0.7756/61 after starting at US$0.7760/65 from US$0.7749/54 late here Wednesday.
Support had proved solid at US$0.7738 on Wednesday despite substantial selling from various offshore sources and dealers expected it to remain a floor for the short term.
Equally, fresh offers were lined up at US$0.7770 and the week's 78 cent high looked set to be the ceiling for a while.
The situation was confused on the crosses where the currency leapt higher offshore when a US$ rally caught the market short, only to be buffeted later by a Japanese rush out of DEM/Yen.
Traders said Japanese investors looked to be repatriating funds out of the mark and into yen to bolster their books before the financial year-end on March 31.

That trend dragged the local dollar back to 93.93/03 yen by the close after initially rising to 94.89 yen this morning from 93.62/72 late Wednesday. But it pressed higher on the ailing mark to 1.3100/14 from 1.2937/51 late yesterday and made gains on the Swiss franc and Canadian and New zealand dollars.
This helped keep the currency up at 59.3 in trade weighted terms from a previous 59.1 finish.
And rising domestic yields promised to underpin the gains.
The entire bond curve shifted higher after Fed chairman Greenspan routed Treasuries with his unsually direct warning that rates might have to rise to head off inflation.
The local market assumed a U.S. tightening would make it even less likely policy would be eased here, and could even heighten the chance Australian rates would follow.
With that in mind the 90-day bank bill future for December dipped five basis points to 93.31, implying a rate of 6.69 percent against the present official rate of 6.0 percent.
Today's domestic data, however, suggested the market could be getting ahead of itself once again.
The benign outlook for inflation was reinforced by another soft set of private sector wages data which showed Q4 annual pay growth slowed to 2.8 percent from 3.5 percent in Q3.
Analysts said the result would reassure the Reserve Bank it's forecast of underlying inflation of around 2.0 percent through 1997 was not in danger.
The outlook meant there should be room to ease if the RBA wanted, but strength in investment suggested one was not needed.
December quarter data on captial expenditure were actually softer than expected with real spending falling 2.4 percent against estimates of a 2.1 percent rise.

But analysts emphasised all the drop was in the volatile building sector where a number of projects had been deferred or were running late. Survey projections for 1996/97 and 1997/98 also remained strong suggesting the Q4 softness was just a blip.
"The positive intentions for business investment suggests (RBA) Governor Macfarlane's 'rates on hold' strategy is a wise one," said Su-Lin Ong, fixed-interest economist at Hambros.

"Given uncertainty on the wages front and a strengthening economy on the horizon, it would take a significant deterioration in the growth and labour market outlook to change the Governor's mind," she said. -- Wayne Cole 61-2 9373 1800
